section_1.title: Intuitive Hook: The Perspective Shift
section_1.content: Introduce the concept of a coordinate system as a 'language' to describe space. Use an animation of a robot (Robby) moving in a room. Explain that the same location in the room can be described by different grid systems (Standard Basis vs. Non-Standard Basis).
section_1.example: A robot marks a point on a floor grid. If the grid lines are rotated by 45 degrees, the robot's (x, y) coordinates change, but the physical location remains identical.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Review: Basis as Building Blocks
section_2.content: Briefly define a basis as a set of linearly independent vectors that span the space. Use graphical representation: showing vectors i=(1,0) and j=(0,1) as the default 'standard' grid, then showing two alternative vectors u and v to form a 'tilted' grid.
section_2.example: Standard Basis: { (1,0), (0,1) }; Alternative Basis: { (1,1), (-1,1) }. Visualizing the vectors as arrows defines the new 'ruler' scale.

section_3.title: The Change of Basis Matrix (P)
section_3.content: Explain that to translate coordinates from the new basis back to the standard basis, we build a transition matrix P. Show the columns of P as the coordinates of the new basis vectors expressed in the standard basis.
section_3.example: If our new basis vectors are u=(1,1) and v=(-1,1), the transition matrix P is [[1, -1], [1, 1]]. Multiplying P by a coordinate vector in the new basis maps it directly to standard Cartesian space.

section_4.title: The Conversion Algorithm
section_4.content: Formalize the process: [x]_std = P * [x]_new. Explain the reverse operation: to go from standard back to new, we need P-inverse. Visualize this as the 'un-warping' of the grid.
section_4.example: If a bird is at [2, 1] in the 'tilted' basis, calculate its standard coordinates by P * [2, 1]^T. Then calculate the inverse to show how the system is reversible.

section_5.title: Application and Conclusion
section_5.content: Summarize how changing basis simplifies complex problems (e.g., Eigenvalue decomposition, computer graphics rotations). Reiterate that changing basis is simply changing our point of view, not the underlying object.
section_5.example: In a 3D game engine, changing basis allows developers to calculate physics relative to an object’s local 'forward' vector rather than the static world map.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=20, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 1.5 + j * 0.8
                y = 2.0 - i * 0.8
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
